name: The Persistence of Memory
kicker: Dalí’s painting of melting clocks · A Surrealist icon at MoMA
briefing: In 1931, Spanish artist Salvador Dalí painted _The Persistence of Memory_, a dreamlike scene of limp, melting watches draped over a dead tree, a table’s edge, and a strange sleeping face. Dalí later said the soft clocks came to him after watching a wheel of Camembert cheese melt in the sun. Now owned by the Museum of Modern Art in New York, this small canvas remains one of the most recognizable Surrealist paintings ever made.

tossups.p: The cliffs in the background of this painting resemble the Catalonian coastline near Cap de Creus, not far from the artist’s childhood home. A dead, bare olive tree stands on a platform at the left side of the scene, with one soft watch draped over its branch.
tossups.r: Its creator, born in Figueres, Spain, was only twenty-seven years old when he finished it. For 10 points, name this 1931 Surrealist painting of melting clocks by Salvador Dalí.

tossups.p: Ants crawl across a hard, often orange watch at this painting’s lower left corner, while three soft, melted watches are draped elsewhere across the scene. A monstrous, melting face lies across the middle of the composition and may be a self portrait of the artist.
tossups.r: That artist claimed the idea came to him while watching a wheel of Camembert cheese melt in the sun. For 10 points, identify this 1931 Surrealist painting of limp clocks by Salvador Dalí.

tossups.p: This painting’s creator reworked its scene in 1954, scattering it into floating, brick-shaped pieces that some link to his postwar fascination with atomic physics; that reworking also adds a large, flattened fish. A soft watch drapes over the edge of a table near the center of the original scene.
tossups.r: Art historians have connected its soft, drooping timepieces to Einstein’s then-recent theory of relativity. For 10 points, name this dreamlike painting of melting clocks, a Surrealist work by Salvador Dalí.

tossups.p: Despite its fame, the original canvas of this painting is tiny, measuring only about nine and a half by thirteen inches. Its creator, part of the European Surrealist movement, painted the fantastical scene with meticulous, realistic brushwork rather than loose or messy strokes.
tossups.r: The painting is sometimes known by a Spanish-language title rather than its English one. For 10 points, name this 1931 Surrealist painting, now at the Museum of Modern Art, showing watches melting across a desert landscape, created by Salvador Dalí.

tossups.p: A dead, bare olive tree holds one soft watch on its branch at the left of this scene, while another soft watch drapes over a table’s edge nearby. The cliffs in the background echo the Catalonian coast near Cap de Creus.
tossups.r: Its creator once said a melting wheel of cheese inspired the soft timepieces here. For 10 points, name this 1931 painting of melting clocks by Spanish Surrealist Salvador Dalí.

tossups.p: This painting’s creator, who elsewhere used crawling ants as a symbol of decay, reworked this scene in 1954 into a version broken into floating, brick-shaped blocks, adding a large flattened fish. Some observers connect that later blocky style to his fascination with atomic physics after the Second World War.

trap.title: The clocks or the painter?
trap.body: Two mix-ups sink this tossup. First, Dalí painted a 1954 reworking of this same scene called _The Disintegration of the Persistence of Memory_, which is a different answer line. Second, clues about the artist’s own life, like his birthplace or his other paintings, describe Salvador Dalí, the painter, not this one painting.
trap.fix: If the clues describe the artist’s biography, say “Salvador Dalí.” If the clues describe melting clocks, ants, and a dreamlike desert, give the painting’s full title, not just “Dalí” or “disintegration.”
trap.line: Real answer line: The Persistence of Memory [or La persistencia de la memoria]
